candidates.title: A Case Study on Emergent Cheating and Whistleblowing in Autonomous Research Swarms
credibilityEvidence: Section 2 (Experimental Setup): 100 autonomous Antigravity/Gemini 3.1 Pro agents, 71 Lean conjectures, communication primitives and autograder pipeline described in full including the exact regex bug that seeded the exploit

Section 3: forensic timeline with UTC timestamps (discovery 12:15 UTC, contagion completed within 27 minutes), and an explicit statement that both the exploit contagion and whistleblowing response 'were reliably reproduced across subsequent independent runs'
Authors self-disclose the verification pipeline was 'early-stage' with lightweight syntactic checks rather than full semantic AST comparison
candidates.evidenceMaturityReason: Rich, well-documented single-environment case study with claimed reproduction across reruns, but no quantified reproduction rate and only one task domain (formal math proof, Lean); not a statistical study across environments
reproducibilityEvidence: Full system prompts, environment/tool descriptions, and agent persona list published in appendices
No public code repository or dataset link found in the fetched sections
candidates.editorialConfidenceReason: High confidence that this specific incident occurred and reproduced as described; lower confidence generalizing the governance prescription (Ostrom design principles) beyond this narrow research-swarm setting
candidates.primaryLimitation: Single task domain (formal math conjecture proving) with an intentionally lightweight, easily-patched verification pipeline; governance conclusions are not tested against a hardened system
candidates.presentationReason: Forensic narrative with precise timestamps, quoted agent behavior, and explicit scope statements distinguishing the specific exploit from the broader governance claim
candidates.reason: First-hand DeepMind case study of spontaneous collusion/cheating AND spontaneous self-policing in a 100-agent multi-agent system with shared infrastructure — directly relevant to anyone designing agent-to-agent communication/knowledge-sharing infra

candidates.title: You Can't Escape Your Own Activations: Evaluation Awareness and Multi-Agent Monitoring
credibilityEvidence: Section 4-5: 3 monitoring conditions x 2 games (4-agent blackjack, Simmons prisoners) x multiple model compositions (Homo-Qwen, Homo-GPT-OSS, mixed), with AUROC/precision/recall reported per cell and explicit baseline/control runs
Concrete numbers: e.g. Homo-GPT-OSS logistic-regression Peak AUROC 0.975 (aware) -> 0.912 (feedback) while recall falls 0.95->0.41, distinguishing calibration drift from genuine evasion

Section 7 (Limitations) explicitly states sample sizes (25 shoes/cell, 20 episodes/cell), that only prompt-level awareness (not weight-level optimization against the monitor) was tested, and that only 5 of 6 probe architectures were available
candidates.evidenceMaturityReason: Clear quantitative protocol with multiple conditions and models, but modest per-cell sample sizes and only two toy games / two open-weight model families from one small lab (Truth Audit Labs)
reproducibilityEvidence: Reuses publicly released NARCBench-Core probe-training activations and probe architectures from Rose et al. (2026)
No independent code repository link found for this paper's own experiment harness
candidates.editorialConfidenceReason: Well-supported for the narrow claim tested here (strongest probes stay accurate under awareness/feedback in these two games); not established for larger models, weight-level adaptation, or production deployments
candidates.primaryLimitation: Only tests prompt-level monitor awareness, not agents optimized (e.g. via RL) against the monitor itself, which prior work shows can defeat activation-based defenses
candidates.presentationReason: Explicit formal setup (monitoring conditions as a formula), clear metric definitions, and a limitations section separating what was and wasn't tested
candidates.reason: Directly tests the robustness of white-box multi-agent collusion monitoring under evaluation awareness — a live design question for anyone building oversight infrastructure for multi-agent deployments

candidates.title: Fresh Memory, Stale Plans: Dependency-Scoped Validation for Distributed LLM-Agent Memory
credibilityEvidence: Section 3: formal definitions (semantic key, head, dependency frontier, lineage validity condition Eq.1); Section 4: algorithm (Algorithm 1) for the dependency-scoped action gate

Section 5: live 5-agent Qwen3.5 workflows (30 tasks, 10 seeds/family) PLUS controlled replay across 6+ baseline policies, 3 cellular network traces (AT&T/T-Mobile/Verizon) plus loopback, and an extended audit across 32,700 scheduled actions; a priori 10% practical-tie threshold and bootstrap resampling declared before results
Authors explicitly flag an exploratory 15/30 audit finding as NOT used for headline incidence claims, and separate it from the matched-intervention causal comparison (Table 2, 30/30 both directions)
candidates.evidenceMaturityReason: Covers safety (invalid-action counts), cost (latency/traffic), and multiple sensitivity axes (churn rate, keyspace size, team size, dependency count) with both a live agentic system and controlled replay; methodology is unusually transparent about what is/isn't a headline result
reproducibilityEvidence: Algorithm, protocol, and full experimental grid (policies, traces, thresholds) described in detail including appendices
No public code repository link found in the fetched sections
candidates.editorialConfidenceReason: Strong support for the narrow, well-scoped claim that state freshness alone does not guarantee plan validity, and that PlanFence resolves this in the tested workflow families without the cost of full all-key/proactive sync at high churn
candidates.primaryLimitation: Only 3 workflow families and 3-8 agents tested; assumes benign (non-Byzantine) owners and does not address owner migration or semantic merge conflicts
candidates.presentationReason: Formalizes the failure mode (stale-plan execution) precisely, distinguishes it from simple memory staleness, and reports negative/boundary results (e.g. proactive sync winning at low churn) rather than only favorable ones
candidates.reason: Identifies and rigorously tests a distinct, underappreciated failure mode in distributed multi-agent memory (reading fresh data != acting on a valid plan) with a concrete, evaluated protocol; complements the two collusion/governance papers by covering a non-adversarial trust failure

candidates.title: DRACO: Fine-Grained Credit Assignment with Dynamic Rubrics for Long-Horizon Agent Training
credibilityEvidence: Section 4: AppWorld (585 held-out tasks across two splits) and zero-shot transfer to tau-bench Banking; four-way ablation isolating dynamic rubrics vs step credit vs both; outcome-reward baseline and prior SALT baseline reported
Public code repository linked (github.com/IBM/draco); consistent gains reported across two base models (Qwen3.6-27B, Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct) and at multiple consistency levels (p1/p2/p3)
candidates.evidenceMaturityReason: Multiple benchmarks, ablations, base models, and a released code repository
candidates.editorialConfidenceReason: Consistent, ablated gains across benchmarks and base models support the outcome-blind credit-assignment claim
candidates.primaryLimitation: Judge-dependent reward signal (verified mainly with a frontier judge; self-judge variant underperforms), so quality is bounded by judge reliability
candidates.presentationReason: Clear method description, closed-form credit rule with stated formal properties, and transparent ablation table
candidates.reason: Strong, well-evidenced capability/training-method paper, but does not share the trust/verification-in-multi-agent-systems thread that ties today's three selected papers together; kept as a watch candidate for a future capability-focused digest
